extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical political economy; economists and historians studying value, rent, and mining economics
extracted.subtask_description: Canonical principles from Adam Smith explaining the origins and determinants of rent, how food production drives demand and division of labour, and how fertility, situation, and scarcity govern prices of land produce, coal, metals, and precious stones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportability and exportability determine rent for produced materials
rubrics_metrics.description: If materials (e.g., clothing materials) cannot be usefully exported and are superabundant locally, much of them become worthless and afford no rent to the landlord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials that readily enter foreign commerce can sustain value and rent; locally-bound materials that are superabundant often afford no rent (example: abundant clothing materials in an inward-trading country).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local market access/situation determines value of lodging materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials of lodging (stone, timber) are less transportable and their value (and rent) depends strongly on local situation, population density, and transport infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good stone quarry near London yields considerable rent; in remote Scotland it may afford none. Improvements in demand elsewhere (e.g., London paving) can create new rents for distant resources if transport permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population depends on food production capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Countries' population size is set by how many people their produce can feed, not by how many they can clothe or lodge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When food is available, clothing and lodging are easier to obtain; thus food production is the primary constraint on population and economic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surplus food enables division of labour and demand for non-food goods
rubrics_metrics.description: When improved land allows one family to produce food for more than itself, surplus labour is employed producing clothing, lodging, furniture, ornaments, etc., increasing demand for materials and division of labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if one family's labour produces food for two, the 'other half' of society can specialize in non-food production, increasing demand for many materials and supporting more workmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlimited appetite for conveniencies vs. limited appetite for food
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire for conveniences and ornaments (building, dress, equipage) seems unlimited, whereas desire for food is limited by the human stomach; hence surplus food tends to be exchanged for endless non-food gratifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why those with surplus food exchange it for extensive non-food consumption; producers compete on quality and price to satisfy rich consumers' fancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food is the original source of rent
rubrics_metrics.description: The rent of land originally derives from food production; later parts of land produce that afford rent derive their value from improvements in labour productivity in producing food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvements increasing food abundance raise demand (and thus value) for other land produce which then may afford rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not all produce that can afford rent will always do so
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a non-food produce affords rent depends on circumstances like fertility and situation; even in improved countries demand may be insufficient to cover labour and replacement of stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include coal, timber, and minerals—some years or places they afford rent, others they only cover costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fertility and situation jointly determine a mine's ability to afford rent
rubrics_metrics.description: A mine's rentability depends partly on its fertility (quantity per labour) and partly on its situation (access to markets and transport).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fertile but remote mines may be unworkable; less fertile but well-situated mines may be profitable. Coal mines illustrate situation sensitivity; metallic mines depend more on fertility because metals bear long carriage costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of fertile vs barren mine
rubrics_metrics.description: A mine is fertile if a given quantity of labour yields more mineral than the same labour would at most other mines; barren if it yields less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fertility is a relative measure compared to other mines of the same kind and governs relative rents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some mines pay only undertaker's profit, not landlord's rent
rubrics_metrics.description: Mines whose produce only suffices to pay labour and replace stock (with ordinary profits) afford profit to the undertaker but no rent to the landlord; often such mines can be worked only by the proprietor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many coal mines in Scotland were historically worked only by landlords themselves because no one else could afford to pay rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport costs and local demand limit distant mines' competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Bulk commodities (like coal) cannot bear high carriage costs, so distant mines' output often cannot compete; precious metals can bear long carriage and compete globally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of transport limits, local most-fertile mines regulate prices for bulk commodities; precious metals' markets are world-wide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most fertile mine tends to set price and can depress neighbors' rents
rubrics_metrics.description: The most fertile nearby mine can undersell others; proprietor and undertaker may prefer selling larger quantities at somewhat lower price, compelling neighbors to follow and reducing their rents and profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resulting competition can force some mines to be abandoned or worked only by proprietors; explains rent variability among mines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum sustainable price equals replacement of stock plus ordinary profits
rubrics_metrics.description: The lowest long-term price of any commodity is that which just replaces the stock used and yields ordinary profits to the undertaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At mines that afford no rent, the commodity price will generally approximate this cost-of-production floor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rent shares differ across land produce categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Rent forms a larger share of gross produce for surface estates (≈ one-third) than for mines (coal commonly one-tenth; a fifth would be very high).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, land estates and mines have different capital valuations (e.g., 30 years purchase vs 10 for mines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Precious metals' price influenced by global most-fertile mines
rubrics_metrics.description: Prices of coarse and precious metals are influenced by the most fertile mines worldwide; yields from the richest mines affect prices at all others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discoveries (e.g., Peru) can depress European mines; hence rents at many mines are small because global supply from fertile mines sets the price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand roots for precious metals: utility, beauty, and scarcity
rubrics_metrics.description: Demand for precious metals arises partly from utility (durability, cleanliness), but principally from beauty and scarcity—beauty enhanced by rarity and the labour required to collect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These qualities made metals suitable for coinage, and coinage itself later increased demand by creating a new use and reducing availability for other uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precious stones' value derives almost entirely from beauty and scarcity
rubrics_metrics.description: Precious stones are demanded as ornaments; their beauty (and the expense/difficulty of obtaining them) is the origin of their high price, with wages and profit composing most of that price and rent often negligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even very fertile gem mines may be left unworked if smaller stones aren't worth the working costs (example: Golconda & selective royal closures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes and policy alter mine profitability and effective rent
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes (royal or ducal) on mine produce can change whether mines can be worked and who receives the economic surplus; high taxes can render previously profitable mines unworkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Spanish crown's tax on silver (once 1/5, later reduced to 1/10) and duke of Cornwall's tin tax (~1/20) affected relative attractiveness and smuggling incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gold is relatively easier to smuggle and separate than silver, reducing captured rent
rubrics_metrics.description: Because gold is often found 'virgin' and separable with simple operations (mercury), it is more prone to smuggling and private extraction, so official taxes and landlord rents form smaller shares of gold's price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technical property of metal extraction affects effective taxation and rent capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute vs relative fertility: estates above ground vs mines
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface estates' value depends on absolute fertility (a given quantity of produce supports a given number of people) and is positively affected by nearby improvement; mines' rent depends on relative fertility compared to other mines worldwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus improvement of neighbouring land often raises the value of barren land (via market creation), whereas discovering superior mines elsewhere can devalue existing mines even if local conditions improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of global supply/demand on metal prices over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Three possible long-run combinations: if demand (market improvement) outpaces supply, metal value rises relative to corn; if supply outpaces demand, metal value falls; if they increase proportionally, relative price remains stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: silver price fluctuations across four centuries owing to discoveries (e.g., Americas) and market changes; this framework explains long-term metal price trends.
